utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in the courtroom. I think I should note the following fact: I was told this morning that this is day 200 in this trial. I think we did a lot of work, and I'm very grateful that we had such a good working atmosphere in the courtroom. The contribution of the parties and the whole staff for the successful trial is really appreciated. We should note that, and we should continue in that way and try to finish the trial successfully. Is there anything to discuss before the witness will be brought in? Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, everyone. Yes, Mr. President, I -- the Prosecution very much appreciates the pace that the Court has set with this trial. It's been a good, tough pace, but I think it's been just right, from the Prosecution's perspective. I've had a chance to speak briefly with Mr. Gajic this morning about a document Mr. Vanderpuye reminded me about. Before General Savcic left the stand, Mr. Vanderpuye was questioning him on a MUP statement he had given. It was on 23 June 2011, at transcript 15980 to 81, relating to Mr. Pecanac. Mr. Vanderpuye meant to offer it into evidence, but as you recall, General Savcic left and then we decided it wasn't needed to recall him. So if I could offer 65 ter 7440 into evidence. And I've been able to discuss this briefly with Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as far as the statement of Mr. Savcic is concerned, the Defence has no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The document will be received into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 7440 shall be assigned Exhibit P2523. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just as a reminder, we left off at 65 ter 56, which was at tab 103, and I'll be continuing on that for a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Butler. Welcome back to the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The affirmation to tell the truth still applies today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, we're still on -- it should be tab 103 in your binder. We already have it in the e-court. It's Mr. Vasic, the chief of the Zvornik CJB's report -- one of his reports of 12 July. You told us briefly about point 1, who Miroslav Deronjic was. Point 2 is a reference to: "A meeting with General Mladic and General Krstic was held at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters at," I think it says, "0800 hours in which tasks were assigned to all those involved." How, if at all, does this fit into your opinion about General -- about the army and the command relationship between the MUP?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I believe this particular sentence again reflects the fact that the police forces there are taking their orders from the senior army commanders on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And then let's just look down it. We see number 3: "The Turks are fleeing towards Suceska, while the civilians are gathered in Potocari." I think we've heard quite a bit about that. Number 4 is talking about setting up a police station in Srebrenica, which I don't think we need to go into. Number 5, it's: "A meeting will begin at 1000 hours with representatives of UNPROFOR and the International Red Cross ..." It talks about: "... an agreement will be reached on the evacuation of the civilian population from Potocari to Kladanj." What meeting, in your view, does this refer to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This refers to what we call the third meeting that occurred at the Hotel Fontana between the VRS, the Dutch Battalion members, and the Muslim representatives from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And number 6: "Joint police forces are advancing on Potocari with the aim of taking UNPROFOR personnel prisoner, surrounding the entire civilian population and cleansing the area of enemy troops." So from the documents and your knowledge, have you an opinion whether or not at this -- at this time, that joint police forces were advancing on Potocari?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And, in fact, at the time or shortly after this 8.00 meeting, Special Police forces did advance towards Potocari, breaching the minefield with some help from the engineers, and their actions were as described.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was Mr. Borovcanin, who we've heard was a deputy commander of the Special Police, involved in this action?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And will we, a little bit later on in our chronology, see some reports from Mr. Borovcanin describing this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I'd offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 56 shall be assigned Exhibit P2524. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And let's now go to 65 ter 2231. It's a similar report from Mr. Vasic. In fact, this last one was number 277. This current one that's coming up is number 278. It's two pages in English, and it's not very legible in the B/C/S. So I have concluded it's from Vasic, but we do see, in the English, "The chief of the CJB."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So can you remind us, who was the chief of the CJB, whose name should have been under that that we can't quite see?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That should be Dragomir Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then looking at this report, we see it's in a similar setup as the last one, and it talks about now: "At 1030 hours, a meeting was held at the hotel in Bratunac, attended by the following:" And we see the group that it's talking about. And is that the meeting that we see parts of on this video that is an exhibit in the case?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, although I should note that the individuals listed in line A representing the Serb side, there were clearly, as the video shows, many more members of the VRS and the Drina Corps present at that meeting than are actually listed by Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you remind us who some of those other key players are that are seen in the video?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Off -- off of memory: General Krstic, I believe Colonels Kosoric and Popovic, Colonel Jankovic is there, General Mladic is there. That's -- from the military side, that's all I recall at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And, B, it says Colonel Karremans was there. Was there some other DutchBat personnel there as well, in your view, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do recall from the videotape that there were several other Dutch Battalion members. I believe Major Franken was -- either Major Franken or Rava [phoen] or Boering was present, one of those two, and then Sergeant-Major Rava was also there. I think it was -- Boering was the officer present with Colonel Karremans.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, we've got the video for that. And we see the Muslim representatives listed as well. And can you remind us what happened if you -- to Ibro Nuhanovic after these days, if you remember or recall, and his wife.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be fair at this point, I don't recall what happened to Mr. Nuhanovic and his wife at this juncture. It's been too many years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at the conclusions: "According to the Muslims ..." We need to go over in the B/C/S, I believe: "... there were 25.000 people in the base in Potocari (mainly small children, women and elderly) and only 10 per cent are conscripts from 17 to 60 years old." What do you make of this comment to his superiors about men from 17 to 60 years old that Vasic is putting in this report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the critical underlying issues for the army at this point in time and, in fact, for the previous evening hours, was trying to determine where were the men of the 28th Infantry Division, what were they doing, and a lot of efforts to get intelligence. When one looks at the military dispositions, the VRS, going into the early-evening hours of the 11th of July and the early-morning hours of the 12th of July, was looking for the 28th Infantry Division and expected to find the remnants of the division in an area of the former enclave known as the Bardera [phoen] Triangle. As we've indicated in earlier intercepts, in fact, they're not in the Bardera Triangle. The division is starting to assemble into this column and start to excultrate [sic] from the enclave. This word and this realisation obviously takes time from the people on the ground who are observing it before it finally makes its way to the leadership of the VRS so they can react to it. Again in this particular context, they are asking the Muslim representatives, Where are the members of the 28th Division, where are all the able-bodied men? And the response is -- that they're getting back in Potocari is that there aren't enough able-bodied men there and none of them are military members, as far as they're able to determine. So this is all part of this larger question of: Where are -- where is the 28th Infantry Division, where are the military-aged men, and what actions are they doing right now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you recall whether the evidence has indicated if Mladic said anything at this 10.00 meeting about doing anything with the able-bodied men roughly 16 to 60 years old, or thereabouts, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What is your recollection?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mladic had indicated that there would be some form of a vetting process for the men of this particular age group in order to ensure that they had not been involved in crimes against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And a separation of able-bodied men to be interviewed, reviewed, and vetted for possible war criminals, is there anything wrong with that, in your view?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. And, in fact, during the morning hours of 12 July, the Bratunac Brigade Intelligence and Security shop actually produced a list of Bosnian Muslims who they believed were involved with crimes against the Serbs, so there was actually a list by which to start vetting these people against. That is a legitimate act.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, as evident in the case, that men were separated and detained, is there any indication that they were provided with the appropriate logistical support of food, water, medicine, support, that -- well, as you see was required by law? And I'm talking about the Potocari men, able-bodied men.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. The only -- the only people who were provided that were those men who were wounded and were under the Dutch care, medical care, and then were transported to Bratunac, where they remained under observation of the Dutch. If you weren't a member of that group, as the investigation has determined, you were put in a number of facilities in Potocari. Your identification was taken away from you, as well as all your other personal goods, and then you were part of that process that ultimately went from Potocari, through Bratunac, and then to various sites in Zvornik where they were subsequently executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's now look at this. As we go down, number 2 says: "They want to leave the camp voluntarily and go to Tuzla or Kladanj, and they request assistance." We'll leave that for consideration to others. Number 3: "They also request free passage for able-bodied men because, allegedly, they are unarmed and they are not in contact with their army in the woods." So which able-bodied men are these, in your view?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are Bosnian Muslim men from the enclave who fall within the age bracket; in this case, 17 to 60. Many [Realtime transcript read in error "men"] of them are not associated with the 28th Infantry Division. What the Muslim representatives are noting at this juncture is that there are two separate groups. One group is an army group, and another group is just Bosnian Muslim men who are seeking to flee, but who are not combatants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I ask you for a clarification. Did you say "many of them are not associated with the 28th Infantry Division" or did you say "men of them"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Many, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most of -- the size of the 28th Division, in terms of manpower, was actually larger than the amount of weapons that the units had available. So, generally, they had more soldiers, and the practice in the enclave was that when one group of soldiers went off duty, another group of soldiers would come in and take those weapons. So the fact that there are unarmed men in the woods is not the same as saying they're not soldiers, so that's why I have to be careful and differentiate between, you know, those individuals who are armed members of the 28th Division, those individuals who are soldiers -- who are members of the 28th Division but, because of circumstances, are not armed, and then the third body, which is men who fall into that able-body range but who are -- and have no association with the military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that third group you mentioned, were any of those in Potocari at the 12th of July, if you know?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I would say that many of those men in Potocari were not associated with the military, and because they had no military association, they chose to accompany their families to Potocari rather than flee into the woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And number 4: "It was decided to grant their requests, and with UNPROFOR assistance (presence and provision of fuel for transportation) and the trucks provided, boarding of vehicles will commence at 1400 hours and the escort will be provided 'til Kladanj." Do you recall yesterday a document from General Zivanovic, where he did not know the final destination of the group?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Does this indicate by the morning of the 12th there is a destination? Is this related to -- I should say: Is this related to the same subject that Zivanovic was talking about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I think if you look in time, General Zivanovic's message relating to acquiring the buses comes several hours prior to this particular document which reflects that a decision has been made where they are going.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then this line: "After the inspection, depending on Mladic's decision, able-bodied men may be allowed to go in order to have the others from the woods to surrender, since our command urged them to do so." Now, this idea mentioned here, that after the inspection of the able-bodied men, depending on what Mladic decides, they may allow those able-bodied men to go as some sort of impetus to get the men from the woods to come down, is that shown on the video anywhere, these comments from Mladic of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the details of that in the video. It may be there are. I just don't recall them at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you know for a fact where Vasic actually got this from?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This particular line?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And then number 5, we see it's a discussion about President Karadzic setting up forces for a police station in Srebrenica, mentioning the 2nd Company of the Zvornik PJP. He also, in number 6, if we go to the next page in English, mentions the 1st Company is carrying out tasks. Now, you have mentioned the 2nd Company of the PJP and the 1st Company, I think, in relation to Mr. Borovcanin. Can you explain: How is it that Vasic is reporting on these folks, and is this different from Borovcanin's folks? As much as you can tell us on that.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, the command relationships between the police bear some discussion. The 1st Company that he is discussing, of course, is the 1st PJP Company. It is, at that point, under the direct command of Mr. Borovcanin, but they are still Vasic's police. So it would be natural for him to discuss what their role was and what missions they were performing. Of the PJP companies, that is the only PJP company that is specifically -- had been previously re-subordinated to Mr. Borovcanin. The other PJP companies that have been mobilised and are operating around -- in and around Srebrenica and other locations remain subordinate at this juncture to Mr. Vasic, as the head of the CJB. And, of course, in this context, Vasic is taking his orders also from the army, and he's keeping his chain of command and the police forces and police staff informed in detail as to what those orders are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I'd offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 2231 shall be assigned Exhibit P2525. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could go to P1565A. And we'll see that this is an intercept. It's from 12 July, from other documents, but all we see, really, is a transcript of the intercept here. It's at 1240 hours, and it's from Panorama, who is X, and Y, who is barely audible. And we see Y say: "We are starting the evacuation of those who want to go towards Kladanj." And X, from Panorama says: "Okay."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What is Panorama?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Panorama is the telephonic code-name for the Main Staff headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And Y says: "Pass it on ... just let ... provide transportation." X can't be heard. Then Y says: "And reinforce ... with trucks and buses, and a water tank should be sent to give them water and food. This morning we organised it here, we'll give them everything. I talked to them, and we'll accept all of the civilians who want to and they can stay. Those who don't want to can choose where they'll go." X can't be heard. Y says: "Goodbye." First of all, who do you think Y is talking about here? That is, he's providing them with water and food and accepting that they can go or stay.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that Y is talking about the civilian population that is at this time presently in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the next document. That one's already in evidence. This is another intercept 10 minutes later, 1250 hours. It looks like the same channel and the same frequency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I interrupt you for a moment. There is something missing on page 13, line 4. You said, sir, Panorama is the code-name for a certain headquarters. Could you repeat that, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That would be the Main Staff headquarters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: P241 is the next exhibit. It's an intercept, 12 July. It's, as I mention, the same frequency, same channel as the last one, but 10 minutes later, and it's identified by the intercept people of the Tuzla CSB as a conversation between General Mladic and an unidentified male they call X.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And X says: "Go ahead, General." Mladic says : "Have these buses and trucks left?" X says: "They have." Mladic says: "When?" X says: "10 minutes ago." Mladic says: "Good, excellent. Continue to monitor the situation. Don't let small groups of them sneak in. They've all capitulated and surrendered, and we'll evacuate them all, those who want to and those who don't want to." X says: "I understand, General." Mladic says: "Don't issue any statements, and don't interrupt them over the" something" station. We'll open a corridor towards Kladanj." X can't be heard. Mladic says: "Indeed, let it pass there. Take a patrol of ours to wait on the road and move the mines and obstacles ... leave the territory." Looking at both these intercepts together, what do you make of them?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mladic has already decided that everyone will be removed from Potocari, regardless of whether they wish to remain or not. In the earlier conversation, the correspondents who were discussing it were still discussing a situation and, clearly, were not yet aware of the final instructions that General Mladic had issued in this regard. It's obviously natural, in not only a military sense, but in any bureaucratic organisational sense, that there is a certain time lag as orders are passed down the chain of command and that all the relevant individuals who will implement those orders become aware of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's continue in the chronology and go to 65 ter 67. This is a new sort of document for us, I believe, that -- we see that it's from the Republika Srpska MUP, RDB, the State Security Department, Sarajevo. We see who it's to; the deputy minister, personally. And it's from the head of the RDB, Dragan Kijac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I believe you've mentioned this briefly, but can you tell us what this is, who Kijac is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is the head of the RDB, which is the state security apparatus of the Republika Srpska. It is part of the Ministry of the Interior. Just like the army had an intelligence and security apparatus as part of its structure, the Ministry of the Interior also had an intelligence collection and security apparatus, which is the RDB.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is there any indication that the RDB had agents or officers on the ground in and around Bratunac and Potocari on the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I am aware that the investigation has identified several RDB agents in and around Bratunac and Potocari on those dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this paragraph notes that: "Representatives of international humanitarian organisations in Srebrenica sent a report to their head offices on 12 July, saying that that the morning humanitarian situation was 'worse than ever.'" And then it says: "According to the report, the population lacked food, medicine and clothing." Then it estimates the number of people around the battalion at 30.000, and 8.000 more trying to get there. According to military observers, there is not a single armed soldier of the so-called BH among these people. A proposal by the UNPROFOR to provide 20 buses. What does this indicate the SDB has got their hands on when it says that "the humanitarian organisations sent a report" and "according to that report"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It reflects the fact that they obviously have knowledge of what various NGOs or the UN, if the NGOs were reporting through the UN channels, the information that they're reporting up their particular chain of command that somehow the RDB is getting access to that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you know if it was intercepted, or gotten through an agent, or found, or do you have any idea how they got this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I'd offer that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, it will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 67 shall be assigned Exhibit P2526. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would just ask Mr. McCloskey and the witness to slow down a bit, because it takes a while before the interpretation is done or completed. They are about six lines behind the speakers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for this advice. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could go to P1566A. It's another intercept from 12 July, 1305 hours now, from Krstic and Sobat [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us who you think this Krstic and Sobat is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular context, "Krstic" is General Krstic, because as one reads further down the particular intercept, one of the correspondents does address him as "General."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, you called him, the other person, Sobat, but I read "Sobot."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I meant to say Sobot. I see it the same way you do. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Does that name, Sobot, ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is an officer on the Drina Corps staff who's associated with the logistics or rear services branch.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see "Krsmanovic." In your view, is that the same Krsmanovic you've already talked about related to buses?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I don't want to go through all of this and who the various folks are, Savo and Kosoric and all, but we see, as we get down, it's talking about a tunnel, and that's where they'll be disembarking, "take care that nothing must happen to them." Can you tell us what it is you think General Krstic is discussing here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular intercept, General Krstic is discussing or being put through to various correspondents the route of the convoy, which brigade areas it will be passing through, and ultimately where the individuals will be dropped off, and then make that final I believe it's one- or two-kilometre walk through the tunnel between the territory of Republika Srpska to the BiH. So this particular conversation is related to making arrangements for those actions to occur.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is it related at all, in your view, to that other conversation we heard where -- that we saw, excuse me, where General Mladic said something like, Clear the obstacles?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What are the obstacles that would need to be dealt with?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were mines and other barriers that had been placed on the road, since there's no traffic that goes back and forth between blinds on that, and this was directions to start taking those barriers down so the people could proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when Krstic says, Take care, nothing must happen to any of them, do you relate that in any way to the -- what we heard from in the -- in General Gvero's document, where he says, Take care of UNPROFOR, there are multiple reasons? Do you -- anything similar or related to these two statements?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, in the sense that while General Gvero was discussing UNPROFOR, in this particular situation General Krstic is seeking to avoid a situation where, particularly close to the demarcation point where the refugees will be placed -- are basically removed from RS territory, he doesn't want an incident or he doesn't want those civilians harmed where they will then immediately make comments and complaints about being harmed by the RS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next document, 65 ter 140. This is a document from the Command of the Drina Corps, the Intelligence Department, on 12 July. It's very urgent, for immediate delivery to the Main Staff Sector for Intelligence and Security, the Intelligence Administration, the Drina Corps Bratunac Forward Command Post, and personally to Lieutenant-Colonel Kosoric.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You've told us who Kosoric is, and we can read the substance of this, so I don't need to go through it. We've heard things like this before. What, basically, is -- and we see this is in the name of Pavle Golic -- "By authorisation of the chief," and it says "Major Pavle Golic." Remind us who Major Golic is.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Golic is an intelligence officer assigned to the Drina Corps Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do we see his name popping up in other intercepts and documents and the Zvornik Brigade duty officer's note-book related to various projects that are going on? I'll say that at this point.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And it makes a reference to the Drina Corps duty officer, a Lieutenant-Colonel Jovicic, and then the operations officer, Lieutenant-Colonel Ognjenovic. Now, if we go back to 1994 briefly and recall the commander of the Bratunac Brigade, a Mr. Ognjenovic, is this Ognjenovic anything to do with the commander of the Bratunac Brigade in 1994 that sent that report to his troops about making life unbearable for the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It is the same person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And are there any documents or intercepts that give us any indication where or what Ognjenovic was doing on these days, 12 or 13 July, that you recall?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. He is performing duties as an operations officer in the Drina Corps Command, Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I would offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 140 shall be assigned Exhibit P2527. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could go to 65 ter 231. And we now come to the Bratunac Brigade Command daily combat report of 12 July that talks about the enemy trying to break through in this particular direction that we see, including Jaglici, Bokcin Potok, towards Tuzla. I don't think that bears any comment at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then number 7: "The transport of the Turkish population (Muslim refugees) from the village of Potocari towards Kladanj is in progress. A large number (10.000) of refugees are expecting to be transported from Potocari to Kladanj." And we see a time handwritten on this, "1430 hours." Does this roughly reflect some of what is going on related to the Muslims of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I would just note it's 12 July at 1630 hours, not 1430 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. My eyes and mouth are not in sync, but hopefully we'll get them in sync. I would offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, it will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 231 shall be assigned Exhibit P2528. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can we go to 65 ter 1985, hopefully briefly, because we see that this is a Main Staff report to the president from 12 July. And if we can go to the Drina Corps section, which is on page 3 of both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we can see in one part that the enemy has been attempting to withdraw from the Srebrenica enclave, with women and children, in the direction of Ravni Buljin and Konjevic Polje, but ran into a minefield. Is this an accurate report, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That particular passage does reflect the knowledge that the Drina Corps has of the current situation and the knowledge that they're obtaining as a result of taking prisoners and interrogating those prisoners for combat information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next page in English. It should still be on page 4 -- page 3 in the B/C/S, page 4 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And under "The Situation in the Territory," it says: "In the Drina Corps zone of responsibility, the population is being taken from Srebrenica enclave to Kladanj in an organised manner. It is estimated on this day that there are about 10.000 Muslims to be transported." Is that, roughly, a correct statement of the situation as it was known by the Main Staff on that day at, roughly, this time-period? We see it's received at 2.00 a.m. on the next day, the 13th.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, again in the context of they're accurately reporting the information that is available to them. I believe that as time goes on, it's clear that the number of individuals leaving Potocari is well in excess of 10.000, but at this juncture the people drafting this particular report don't know that yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, I believe, as I'm noting, that this document is P1215, and for some reason we gave it a 65 ter number. That's the next one in the binder, I see, so I don't think it needs to be offered into evidence. It already is. So unless I'm wrong, could we go to 65 ter 232.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Still on 12 July, a document from the Command of the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade to the Drina Corps Command; attention, Major Golic. Is that the same Major Golic, in your view, that we talked about last time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see some information that is being passed on to Intelligence Officer Golic by a Captain Pecanac. What did you learn about who this Captain Pecanac was at the time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding from the investigation, as well as other documents, reflects that Captain Pecanac is an officer of the VRS Main Staff who is affiliated with the Intelligence and Security Sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I would offer that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'll skip over --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 232 shall be assigned Exhibit P2529. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm going to skip the next tab and go to tab 115, which we have seen before. It's P2203. It's the 12 July document from General Tolimir, talking about various intel information and proposing Muslims going through the woods be arrested? And you've talked on that in a previous section. It's just here as a place holder, so I don't think we need to discuss it again. I'll go on to the next document, which is D64. And as the previous document, this is a 12 July document from General Tolimir that you've spoken before, where he talks about intel information and makes proposals about capturing Muslim men. And this is where he notes that it's important to note down the names of all men fit for military service who are being evacuated from the UNPROFOR base in Potocari. It's already been discussed, so if we could go past that now to 65 ter 168? And this, as we will be able to see on the screen soon, is from the 1st Milici Light Infantry Brigade, the Security Affairs organ to the Drina Corps Command, the OB department. And it mentions at 1600 hours, in the area of Buljim, the person got away from a group of soldiers heading away from Srebrenica, and it lists the person's name, Ibis Malic, son of Maso, born 1 January 1977, and it provides information. Can you tell us, just briefly, what this is? I don't need -- we're familiar with the information now, but just what's the Milici Brigade doing here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Milici Infantry Brigade had defence positions around parts of the former enclave. This is just simply a reflection of a soldier who surrendered to the Milici Brigade, his, you know, interrogation after surrendering, where combat information is obtained from him, and the reporting process by the Milici Brigade to their higher command, the Drina Corps Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I would refer you to the report of Dusan Janc and the ICMP identifications to find out the fate of this particular man. I will get a more specific reference for you. But I would offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 168 shall be assigned Exhibit P2530. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And now, getting over to 13 July in the chronology, could we go to 65 ter 762.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we'll see, as we get to it, that this is another report from Dragomir Vasic of the Zvornik CJB, referring to a meeting with General Mladic that morning, where he says: "We were informed that the VRS was continuing operations towards Zepa ..." And in Vasic's words: "... leaving all other work of the MUP as follows:" Is this what happened, roughly?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct. At some point, at a meeting that occurred at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters on the evening of 12 July 1995, various members of the Drina Corps and the Main Staff, at the direction of General Mladic, begin to put together a plan that would rapidly move military units from the areas in and around the former enclave and pivot them, as it were, so they could very quickly undertake military operations against the Zepa enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And during the day on the 13th, did the VRS really understand, in your view, in your opinion, how many Muslim able-bodied men, especially those from the 28th Division, had made it across the Milici-Konjevic Polje-Kravica road into the woods towards Erdut and on towards Baljkovica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. And if one looks at the reporting coming from Major Obrenovic of the Zvornik Brigade and various intercepts that go between the Zvornik commands, Vlasenica, the Drina Corps, and the Main Staff, even, what does become evident is that the senior military officers in the Drina Corps and on the Main Staff have underestimated the number of men in the column, and of obvious most relevance to the Zvornik Brigade, armed men in the column. So while you have a situation where the Zvornik Brigade is talking about a potential crisis, as they have expectations of a rather large military force approaching it and they have no available reserves left, Major Obrenovic's assessments of those situations are generally considered to be over-statements by other members of the army. In fact, Major Obrenovic's assessments are accurate as to the size and the military threat the column posed, and you see that on the late evening of the 14th and early-morning hours of the 15th, when the Drina Corps is forced to start sending military formations from Zepa back to Zvornik in order to reinforce the combat operations that are occurring there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we see number 1 of the tasks that the MUP is doing: "Evacuation of the remaining civilian population from Srebrenica to Kladanj ..." Its estimate is about 15.000 by bus. We see that according to Vasic, petrol is still a problem. And then number 2, it says: "Killing of about 8.000 Muslim soldiers whom we blocked in the woods near Konjevic Polje. Fighting is going on. This job is being done solely by MUP units." And if we look at the Serbian term, it's "likvidacija." What does this statement mean to you? This is a report on 13 July. It's not clear exactly what time it went out, and I think we'll all recall the Kravica warehouse, in the later hours of -- afternoon/evening hours of 13 July, but what has this meant to you over the years, and has your opinion changed at all?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. What this particular phrase represents to me is the combat operations against the -- part of the Muslim column, a significant part of the column, that has not been able to cross the road at Konjevic Polje, between Konjevic Polje and Nova Kasaba, and continue on the way to free territory. "Liquidation" is an interesting phrase that's used. And very early on, because of what it potentially means in English, where it does have a sinister connotation, I did engage with various translators and language experts at CLSS to determine if it had the same sinister connotation in the Serbo-Croat language. They informed me that it, in fact, does not. It's just a term that they use to, you know, reflect doing something, you know, completely -- doing it in its complete -- entirely. So I've always made the point, when coming across those phrases, particularly when it has to do with individuals were being killed, to point out that in this particular context, they're merely talking along the lines of, you know, combat operations to kill the remaining soldiers. It's not read as liquidating soldiers in a more sinister context.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And have you seen the term "liquidating" used when, in fact, they were talking about killing people in a summarily executive way?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I recall since leaving. I mean, normally the term that they use in that context with the intercepts that I'm aware of is they call that particular phrase "triage."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And if we go back on an intercept, I believe it was -- yes, it was the evening of 13 July, where X and Y were talking about a total of 6.000 able-bodied men at three locations in the area. So if we give, roughly, some credence to those 6.000 that would be captured at that point, would those 6.000 be at all related to this reference much earlier in the day of 8.000?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it would encompass the column -- the general estimates of the size of the column are, for a variety of reasons, very difficult to estimate, but I believe I've always been consistent that the column's between 10 and 15.000 people. So those numbers, an 8.000 number, a 6.000 number, of individuals who are involved at that location on 13 July, even those high numbers would be consistent with my understanding of the size of the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But by the evening of 13 July, are a lot of those able-bodied men now POWs?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: More than that, sir. By the evening of 13 July, after the Kravica warehouse, approximately a thousand of them are already dead. There are probably another 2.000 who are on buses and trucks, in the custody of the VRS and of the police, in other locations in and around Bratunac, where they're being held on those vehicles or other locations before they get sent to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do those numbers in Bratunac increase as the evening goes on and more people are being brought in?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. My understanding, based on the ongoing investigation, is that through that particular evening, more vehicles filled with prisoners are being brought in as each hour passes, and there's some manner of difficulty in finding appropriate places to park the vehicles and to properly guard them because they're getting so many of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 762 shall be assigned Exhibit P2531. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. If we could go to P2238.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We now see a report from the Special Police Brigade on 13 July. We don't really see any time reference in the document, aside from what could be gleaned from the document itself. It's to the Pale Police Staff, the Vogosca Police Staff, and the Special Police Brigade, Janja, and it's from Ljubisa Borovcanin, the deputy commander. So, briefly, before we discuss some of the content, what is this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just as Dragomir Vasic sent reports up detailing the situation, so did Ljubisa Borovcanin. This is a report that Mr. Borovcanin sent to his police superiors, detailing the situation on the ground, as he understood it, as well as what activities that the forces under his command were engaged in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is this consistent with the similar topics mentioned by Dragomir Vasic when he talked about joint police forces? I think he said joint police forces are moving towards Potocari, something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. This -- this joint police force that moved towards Potocari was part of Mr. Borovcanin's unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So when Borovcanin says in the course of the day, a MUP force was engaged in the direction of Zuti Most, towards Potocari, what day is he talking about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This activity he is describing is the early-morning hours of 12 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so when he says, There was no strong-armed resistance from the Muslims, so we took control of Potocari by 13 [sic] hours, with the right-hand flank, we took control of the Budak and Milacevici features, was that also 12 July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And his comment about: "In Potocari, we sealed off the main UN base, where a throng of between 25.000 and 30.000 civilians had gathered ..." And he now notes that: "... 5 per cent of whom were able-bodied men." So we now have Vasic talks about able-bodied men on his 12th July report, and now we have Borovcanin. Is that the same able-bodied men that they're both talking about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think their percentages are a bit different? Do you recall Vasic's percentage? If not, don't worry about it, that document is in evidence.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Vasic says 10 per cent. Borovcanin says 5 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He notes that: "A part of the MUP force was involved in the organisation of the evacuation of civilians from Srebrenica ..." And can that be seen from the video of 12 July and 13 July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The videos do show that the various bus convoys are escorted by MUP forces, either Republika Srpska police or other MUP forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Then he talks about how the able-bodied Muslim men set off through Konjevic Polje towards Tuzla, and that he urgently dispatched forces with hardware to seal off the Kravica-Konjevic Polje road. We need to go over to the next page in English. Did the investigation, and Petrovic video, and other information bear out this statement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now he talks about the night between 12 and 13 July, that the armed Muslim group launched an attack in the direction of Konjevic Polje, and that combat lasted several hours and continued through the day. So what day is he now talking about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this juncture, he's now talking about the 13th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And he notes that the enemy sustained a loss of 200 soldiers who were killed, and he notes that: "... we captured or had surrendered to us around 1500 Muslim soldiers." And: "This number increases by the hour." Now, you have discussed the document of 13 July in the name of Savcic, where, according to that document, General Tolimir issues a proposal, and there's a discussion of over 1.000 -- or there's a mention of over 1.000 prisoners in the Kasaba area. Is Borovcanin -- are his units in the Kasaba area at all?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, they are not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us where his guys are, where they're getting these 1500 Muslims in relation to Kasaba?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police forces under Borovcanin's command are essentially staged, literally, in a very long series of lines along the road from the town of Konjevic Polje, back towards Bratunac, to the Sandici Meadow and actually a little bit further towards Kravica in that regard. So the prisoners that he's talking about, because of the territory that he controls, are different from the prisoners that are being accounted for at Nova Kasaba.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And he notes that: "The number increases by the hour." And then he says: "According to all indications, the number of Muslim soldiers who did not manage to break through is on the rise and is approximately between 5.000 and 6.000, which means that we have intense combat ahead of us." So we had just heard that -- I think from Vasic that they were fighting 8.000. Is this 5.000 and 6.000 that he's talking about the same group that Vasic is talking about, or is this a group that's already gone past the road and is on their way towards Zvornik, or some other group?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I believe this is the same group that Vasic was talking about. When one compares the reports of Vasic and Borovcanin, it's clear that they have a pretty common view of what the battle-field situation looks like at that particular time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. And something just I wanted to clear up. I asked you about the previous document, where Vasic makes this reference to liquidating 8.000 people, and I asked you, Had your view of that changed over the years? And I recall that you said, Yes, sir. But when you said, Yes, sir, did that mean your -- what did that mean, when you said, Yes, sir, just so we can clear that up?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said, Yes, sir, as my predicate to answering the question. I did not mean that my opinion of that had changed over the years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I didn't think it had, so I thought I better clear that up. And I would offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think it's in evidence. It's P2238.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Absolutely correct. And the next document is a more lengthy report, so I think this is the -- and it is the time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed. We must have our first break now, and we will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we now go to 120 tab, and it's P1335.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as we're waiting, I'll note that this is from the Republika Srpska Ministry of Interior, Special Police Brigade Bijeljina. It's got a date of 5 September 1995 up in the left corner, and it's entitled: "Report on the Combat Engagement of the Special Police Brigade and Other Police Forces in Operation Srebrenica 95 in the Period from 11 July to 21 July 1995." If we can go to the last page. I don't think we really need to. It's page 5 of the B/C/S, 6 of the English. It says: "Report submitted by: Ljubisa Borovcanin." So, Mr. Butler, I know you've had a chance to review this report. What is this report, briefly?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In September 1995, Mr. Borovcanin is tasked to write a report pertaining to the activities that both he and the units under his direction took related to Srebrenica. This particular document is his report of that situation and the activities that he undertook.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And let's start with it should be page 1 in the English translation - I believe it's page 2 of the B/C/S - where he starts getting into the detail. I want to ask you about a few of these things. It says -- begins: "By order 64/95 issued by the deputy minister of the interior on 10 July 1995, I was sent with some MUP forces to participate in the Srebrenica operation ..." And then it goes on and it lists the forces. Have we seen this order he's referring to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That is the order by acting Minister Kovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we see, as we go down the page, he describes the units that the order entailed, and then he starts describing, in the first paragraph, during the night of 10/11, he came to Jahorina, and starts describing his dealings with people. And can you remind us where he was coming from?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this point in time, he and the police units he was commanding were engaged at the Trnovo battle-front.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see he notes at the bottom of this page that Spaso Skoro, assistant commander for the Special Police Brigade, took over command of the police forces in Trnovo. Was -- how did that relate to Borovcanin?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once Borovcanin, who was commanding those forces, was ordered to a different assignment, there was a requirement to designate somebody else to command the remaining police forces at Trnovo. That would be him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we see on this first page that he basically describes the units that were in the order, and he does mention the Serbian MUP. As you go through this document and he talks about the various units that came with him and what they are up to, do you ever see him report again about anything to do with the Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So what would that indicate to you whether or not they are came with him?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That indicates to me that they did not accompany him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to page 2 in the English. It should be still page 2 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He talks about arriving in Bratunac at 1200 hours on the 11th. He became acquainted with the situation on the front at Srebrenica town, in the direction of Pribicevac. Then he says: "From the observer post in Pribicevac, I contacted General Mladic, who personally commanded over the operation." Is that information consistent with what you had learned about the location of General Mladic on this date?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Pribicevac was the forward command post that the Drina Corps was using for this particular operation, and at some point General Mladic did personally arrive at Pribicevac for the -- at this particular juncture, it would be the last half -- or the last part of the operation, which would include the actual capture of the town of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And it says: "On receipt of combat papers, he ordered me to that same day with all available manpower and equipment from the direction of Zuti Most to Potocari and Milacevici, which was an unrealistic task in view of the fact that the envisaged police forces had still not arrived in this area or could not be used." Now, going back to the issue of whether or not Borovcanin was under the command of the army at this period, does this statement in his report give you any indication on that issue?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I believe it's not unambiguous at all that Borovcanin believes he's under the command of the army and is taking orders from, in fact, General Mladic, the commander of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But we will recall his 10 July order that said he was to, I believe, make himself available to General Krstic. Does this change your analysis, or how would you incorporate that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. General Krstic is the chief of staff of the Drina Corps. And at the time the order was written, he was the man -- the senior army person directing military operations. When General Mladic, as the commander of the army, shows up, by default he is now the senior army officer, and it would be completely customary for Borovcanin to report to General Mladic in this sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what about his statement, saying that Mladic's order was unrealistic because his forces -- Borovcanin's envisaged forces had not arrived or could not be used?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, General Mladic gave him an order of what he wanted to occur. Borovcanin, in this statement, appears to have made the reply that regardless of what he may have told General Mladic, he didn't feel that he had the ability to accomplish that mission, simply because the available forces hadn't arrived in the area yet. He -- in this sense, he obviously went ahead in order to receive his orders. As one notes further in time, as those forces become available, he does undertake this mission, or the mission is modified by General Mladic in the coming hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Remind us what that mission is that he actually did eventually do.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Beginning the morning of 12 July 1995, those particular MUP forces do begin to advance towards -- from the Yellow Bridge area to Potocari, so he's following General Mladic's order. He's just having to wait until he assembles his forces to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then he describes this MUP company from the training centre who you described yesterday. I think you said they had also been referred to as the deserter unit, led by Dusko Jevic and Mendeljev Djuric. Can you tell us briefly about those two folks and whether or not there's other evidence that they were in the area and involved, just very briefly.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. These were the previously-discussed individuals who were undergoing police training at the Jahorina Training Centre. Initially, one company of these police recruits was put together to accompany the forces designated in the 10 July order from Minister Kovac. As it turns out, they were later joined, I believe on the 12th of July, by a second company from the Jahorina Training Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And remind us, where did Dusko Jevic, as assistant commander, and Mendeljev Djuric, company commander, fit into this, as he notes here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dusko Jevic at this time is in charge of the training centre. Mendeljev Djuric is one of the designated deserter company commanders. The name Nedjo Ikonic will also come up. He is another one of the -- he is the 2nd Company commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember the shortened name for Mendeljev Djuric?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. He's referred to as Mane.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you remember the name of Dragomir Vasic's deputy for the Zvornik CSB?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's the same name, Mane Djuric.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is it the same person?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, it is not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please pause between question and answer and the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see that he is ordering the 1st Company of the Zvornik PJP to gather. Do you remember the nickname of Dusko Jevic, as learned by the investigation and, actually, acknowledged by Dusko Jevic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. His nickname is Stalin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I won't go through all of this. But in that paragraph, it's talking about the 1st Company, and he also makes reference to clearing a passage through the minefield, and that there was a team of pioneers from the Bratunac Brigade to clear the passage through the minefield; is that all correct, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then he makes reference that: "At about 2000 hours, negotiations began between Mladic and a representative of UNPROFOR and the Srebrenica Muslims." So this would be 2000 hours. What day is he talking about here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: 11 July 1995, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So what do you think he's referring to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two meetings on the 11th of July. The first one was strictly between General Mladic, the VRS, and representatives of the Dutch Battalion, which took place at approximately 2000 hours. The second meeting, which took place at 2200 hours, included a representative -- a civilian representative of the Bosnian Muslims in Potocari. So since he is talking about Srebrenica Muslims, I take it he's talking about the second meeting that occurred on 11 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then he says: "General Mladic ordered me to launch an attack in the early hours of the following morning." Is this a reference to what Mladic said at Pribicevac, or do you think that it's something later that Mladic has said to him, or can you tell from this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I take this to read that sometime after receiving his initial orders at Pribicevac, he met with General Mladic again later at the Hotel Fontana, I presume, and General Mladic modified the original order and then told Borovcanin that the attack that his forces needed to undertake, you know, could take place in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And then we see that he describes one of these units, the 2nd Special Police Detachment that arrived around 0300 hours. That would have been on the 12th. And that was one of the -- was that one of the units referenced in the original 10 July order?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It is a somewhat complicated military activity to withdraw a unit that's engaged in combat operations, reorganise them, and then send them to a different location on the battle-field. You just can't leave a gap in the line. Somebody has to fill that position. So the fact that it would take a number of hours in order to accomplish this, and then make the unit available to be sent to Srebrenica, is not unsurprising.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And then he describes what happens in the early-morning hours and going through the minefield, and that a member of the Bratunac Brigade set off a mine and died. And then he mentions the first task was to take control of the UN check-point on Zuti Most, and that was completed without any incidents, and that the Dutch members did not react. Is that consistent with a similar comment he made in that just brief report we saw on the 12th and 13th by this same author?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Then he describes the estimate of the number of civilians. And if we go to the next page in English, he talks about this -- the next page in B/C/S as well. He talks about the civilians being transported to Kladanj in an organised way, that it was organised by the army, and that the MUP forces had a supportive role, such as regulating traffic and maintaining public law and order. Then later on, they received information from State Security that 12- to 15.000 able-bodied, mostly armed Muslims were moving from Srebrenica towards Konjevic Polje, Cerska and Tuzla. Is that the group that you've just given your own estimate, based on your experience, was between 10- and 15.000 moving in that direction?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then he tells us he's received an order from General Mladic to send half of his men and available technical equipment to that axis so as to block the area and fight the aforementioned formations. Can you describe to us where, from the evidence, the videos, the documents, Borovcanin took his units?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those particular units moved up to the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road, and as video footage of -- the Petrovic video shows, the bulk of his forces, including a tank and several anti-aircraft vehicles, are in and around the area we refer to as the Sandici Meadow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see that he says the 2nd Special Police Detachment and the 1st Company of the Zvornik PJP, with two tanks, a BOV, a Praga -- and a Praga. The translation describes what a Praga is. It's a self-propelled anti-aircraft gun. Can you tell us what a BOV is, in your view, and what a Praga is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are self-propelled -- they're basically self-propelled crew-serve weapons. The Praga is an anti-aircraft gun. I think the BOV in this particular context that they are referring to is also -- has an anti-aircraft gun mounted on it, if I recall the Petrovic video correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And then in this, he talks a bit about the deployment along the road there, and then he says: "It's estimated that 3- to 4.000 enemy soldiers managed to pass along this segment towards Cerska and further to Sapna and Crni Vrh." You, of course, now have been able to view material after the fact. Who are these estimated 3- to 4.000 people that he's talking about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: More importantly than me, Mr. Borovcanin has had two months to review materials after the operation occurred as well, so he is aware that these 3- to 4.000 soldiers represent the bulk of the armed members of the column that were able to successfully cross the road during the evening hours of the 11th and 12th of July. As, I believe, the evidence has borne out certainly in earlier trials, the military leaders in the column made the decision to place as many of the armed soldiers as they could at the -- or towards the front of the column in anticipation of the fact that that would be where the heaviest combat would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And does -- that 3- to 4.000 number that made it through and headed up in that direction, is that consistent with what you've learned about what Obrenovic was reporting and any other indications from your time in the case?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It is consistent with the numbers that Obrenovic and other members believed were the forces that were approaching the Zvornik area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now we get to 13 July, which should be page 3 in the B/C/S. It's got a very short section, we see, relative to the other days -- to the previous day - excuse me - where he says that the situation was getting more complex because of the advance of the Muslim formation who had managed to break through, so they engaged other forces. I think you've made a reference to that. Traffic was stopped along that road. Then the next paragraph is: "Forces of the Army of Republika Srpska mostly regrouped in order to go to Zepa." Was that correct? Was that what they were doing -- the VRS was doing on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it says: "One member of the Skelani Platoon of the 2nd Police Detachment was killed in the fighting with the enemy." Are you aware of one member of the Skelani Platoon of the Special Police Detachment being killed along that road between Konjevic Polje and Kravica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. He was killed at Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember his name at this point?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And what do you recall the circumstances, just very briefly, of his killing? You say "Kravica." Where?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was -- according to the information derived from the investigation, as well as other information pertaining in medical records or military medical records, he was killed in the town of Kravica. There was no combat in the town of Kravica, but as the evidence of the investigation has noted, he was killed in conjunction with the Kravica warehouse massacre which occurred approximately 1700 hours that day. The information that the investigation is aware of is that he, reportedly, was killed by Muslim soldiers seeking to escape the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. There's quite a bit of material in the record on that, so I think we'll just leave that where it is. In his regular -- or his 13 July report that referenced the 12th and 13 July, he particularly had mentioned that on the 13th of July, around 1500 Muslim soldiers had been captured or surrendered to his forces, and that the number increases by the hour. We don't see any reference to that in this 13 July portion. Do we see any reference to all those surrendered or captured men along that road anywhere in this report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. By September 1995, I suspect that that's an inconvenient fact, and, as such, it was omitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: By September of 1995, the news of the involvement of the Army of the Republika Srpska, and in this context the MUP units of the Republika Srpska serving with the army at Srebrenica, and their association with the massacres had become public. It had started becoming public as early as August of 1995. So for individuals who were involved in that, it wouldn't make much sense for them to create official documents reflecting their association or knowledge of prisoners whom they knew to be dead. And, in fact, not just dead, murdered, in the case of the Kravica warehouse, murdered by forces under his command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. We see, as we continue on page 3 of both languages, a brief comment on the 14th. We've got to go to the next page in B/C/S to catch the 14th - thank you - where he talks about new problems arising, that Zvornik threatened by these Muslim forces from Cerska. Then he talks about the 15th, gives a description of his units and what they're doing, and then again refers to the enemy forces were estimated at 3500 to 4.000 men moving towards Nezuk, was coming behind the soldiers of the Zvornik Brigade along the axis toward Baljkovica. Are these 3500 to 4.000 the same men he's referred to that made it over the road?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Then he talks about fighting throughout the day on the 15th along all the aforementioned axes, and considerable losses were inflicted on the enemy. He says: "All the units remained on the lines reached during the night." Then he says: "The blockade of the area was organised by the Zvornik Brigade." And he says: "We did not 'like' the basic idea because the latest developments, the artillery of the Zvornik Brigade was relocated in a hurry, so that it was still not operational." What's he talking about, if you -- in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, there's a bit of a back story to this particular passage. Sometime during the late evening hours of the 14th of July and the early morning hours of the 15th of July, 1995, Borovcanin and the police forces under his command are ordered to leave the area where they are on the road between Bratunac and Konjevic Polje and deploy into the area of Zvornik, the Zvornik Brigade in order to deal with, as he says, the military threat. At the same time this is occurring, units of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade who are deployed at Zepa, under the command of Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic, are also being ordered back to Zvornik because of the growing military threat. At approximately noon on the 15th of July, at the headquarters of the Zvornik Brigade, there was a meeting of the relevant military and police commanders. Colonel Pandurevic, Major Obrenovic, Mr. Borovcanin, was part of that meeting. Dragomir Vasic was part of that meeting. I believe the commander of the 2nd Sekovici Detachment was also part of that meeting. It was a quick council of war, if you will, where Colonel Pandurevic was updated on the situation that was -- the military situation in his brigade, and where they determined what acts and actions they would take in order to counter that particular situation. From my awareness of previous testimony of Mr. Vasic and statement of Mr. Borovcanin, the police's position was not that they should engage in a military battle against a force that vastly outnumbered even their assembled forces at this point, but that they were advocating that perhaps the Zvornik Brigade should allow the armed head of the column to safely pass between the lines and reach ABiH territory. At that particular meeting, at least according to the recollections of these individuals and Major Obrenovic, Colonel Pandurevic rejected that proposal and, instead, made a determined effort to seek to militarily engage and defeat the column.
