So where he's talking about, We did not like that basic idea, this is Borovcanin now, two months later, expressing the fact that the police leadership at that meeting did not agree with Colonel Pandurevic's plan, although they were obligated to carry it out. And, in fact, they did so to the best their ability.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And in his report, we now come to the 16th, where he describes fierce fighting with the Muslim forces in the area of Krizevici, Tisova Kosa and Baljkovica. And just briefly, did that include Muslim forces from the 28th Division coming from the direction of Srebrenica as well as Muslim forces from the 2nd Corps from the direction of Nezuk?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He describes the Muslim forces capturing three 57-millimetre self-propelled guns of the VRS and firing upon the VRS forces. Then he describes that the VRS had about 40 killed and more than 80 wounded, that 1 member of the 1st Company of the Zvornik PJP was killed and 5 members wounded, and that at about 1500 hours, the bulk of the enemy column, about 2500 soldiers, managed to break through to Nezuk. We need to go to the next page in the B/C/S. But then as he goes on in the English, which is page 5 in the English, if it's the correct translation, he goes back in time and says: "At 1300 hours, the commander of the Zvornik Brigade, Vinko Pandurevic, and the commander of the Muslim side, Semso Muminovic, agreed to open a one-kilometre-wide corridor in the area of Parlog and Baljkovica to allow Muslim soldiers to get out." That this truce would be in force for 48 hours, et cetera, as we read through it. So how do you take this? Do you -- from your knowledge of the reports on this, do you know where large amounts of soldiers -- Muslim soldiers able to break through before this corridor was opened up, or is this a reference to people getting through after the corridor was opened up, but if you know from the -- of course, from the documents, intercepts?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: To a large degree, Borovcanin's description of the ferocity of the combat is accurate, and as well as the members of the army killed and wounded. My understanding, based on my analysis of the other military documents, is not that they were able to break through prior to the cease-fire and the agreement made between Pandurevic and Semso Muminovic. My understanding of the combat situation was that until and up to the point that Colonel Pandurevic agreed to that, the column still had not successfully broken through the VRS lines. So in this particular context, my view has been that Colonel Pandurevic, in making a calculation as to the casualties that his particular unit was incurring against the column, and the reasonable expectation that he would be able to still prevent the column from achieving its mission, he made the decision, and one that was not authorised by his superiors, to allow the column to pass through his lines and go to ABiH territory. Colonel Pandurevic, for his part, attributes a different motive to his reason as to letting the column go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, what do you believe -- or what, in your view, did Pandurevic say regarding his motive for letting the column go, and in what context did he say it? What are you basing that on?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, Colonel Pandurevic, now General Pandurevic, did testify on his behalf during the Popovic trial, and his position was that he allowed this column to pass through, and his decision on the 16th was strictly a humanitarian gesture and had nothing to do with the scope and scale of combat activities that had occurred on the 15th and the 16th. It is, from my perspective, difficult to square that in light of the fact that less than 24 hours prior to the decision to let the column go, Colonel Pandurevic was vetoing advice by police and other individuals that they should let the column go in the first place. In context, he believed that he could make a fight out of it and inflict significant casualties on the enemy. He did. But, in turn, the enemy inflicted significant casualties, in both manpower and materiel, to his brigade. And only when faced with that situation on the afternoon of 16 July, did he unilaterally make the decision to allow the remainder of the armed column to pass safely through his lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you put this in a little context for us? Can you tell us, and just very briefly: What was going on, as well as this fight with the column, in the area of the Zvornik Brigade on the 14th, the 15th and 16th, you know, as charged in the indictment? I don't mean for you to be giving evidence on that. The Court has seen plenty of evidence. But can you remind us: As charged in the indictment, what is going on on the 14th, the 15th and the 16th, in terms of non-combat activity and the involvement or non-involvement of Zvornik -- excuse me, and the involvement of Zvornik Brigade troops?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. As it's laid out, not only is the Zvornik Brigade, during this period starting on the evening of the 13th of July, beginning to engage in combat activities against the armed column, but starting the evening of the 13th July, the first convoy loads of buses and trucks, filled with men from the Bratunac area and those who had been captured, start arriving in the zone of the Zvornik Brigade and are starting to fill up schools in Orahovac, Petkovci, Rocevic and Pilica. So in this particular context, not only is the Zvornik Brigade having to deal with a significantly adverse military situation that is developing in its zone, it is also having to deal with obligations related to guarding and later participating in various aspects of the executions of thousands of Bosnian Muslim prisoners that were in the brigade zone. It created, from a military perspective, a situation where the Zvornik Military Brigade had completely exhausted its reserves and abilities. They were -- to use a phrase, they were flat-out committed. They had no reserves or nothing left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. To finish up this report - I think we're still on page 5 of the English - as we review briefly the rest of these dates, we get down to the 20th of July, the final entries, where he talks about the various people that commanded the units that he was working with; Dusko Jevic, Mane Djuric -- and when he says "Mane Djuric" there, which one do you think he means?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is referring to his subordinate, Mendeljev Djuric, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And Nedjo Ikonic, Milos Stupar, and if we go to page 6 in the English, Rado Cuturic, and the others. Do you recall anything happening to Rado Cuturic on the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Also at the Kravica warehouse, at the same time that the first soldier was killed, he was injured and later taken to the Bratunac Medical Centre, where he received treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember how he was injured or what part of him was injured, if --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I recall correctly, he received a burn on his hand or arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did Mr. Borovcanin tell the investigation how that happened?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, if I recall correctly, Mr. Borovcanin stated that he was injured in this way when he grabbed the rifle barrel of a weapon that a Bosnian Muslim prisoner had obtained while attempting to depart from the Kravica warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And that document is already in evidence, so -- now, that got us a bit out of our chronology because it went all the way through the 20th, so we need to, unfortunately, go back to catch our chronology, which was still on the 13th of July. And if we could do that by getting to P1560B, an intercept. And this is an intercept dated 13 July 1995, at 2040 hours, and it's identified --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It should not be broadcast because it's confidential.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It has been identified as being from General Krstic, and X, who they put in parentheses, is "Borovcanin from the specials." Who do you think this "Borovcanin from the specials" would be?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Ljubisa Borovcanin, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see the conversation between Krstic -- I won't read it all. Borovcanin says: "Hello, this is Borovcanin, General. How are you?" And Krstic says: "Well, where are you, fuck it?" Borovcanin says: "I'm here at the command post." Where would that be, in your view, if you could tell, on the evening of 13 July at 24 [sic] hours? Where would Borovcanin's command post be, in your view, if you have any knowledge?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, given the fact that this conversation is intercepted over the military telecommunications network, the command post that he would be referring to would be the actual -- or former IKM and, in fact, the headquarters of the Bratunac Infantry Brigade in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you say the military network. Could he be at the police command or the police station in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding from the investigation, as well as from the statements by Mr. Borovcanin, was that he was in and around Bratunac and, at one point, at the police station. However, the fact that he's on the military communications network, which I do not believe the police station in Bratunac has access to - they have their own police network - and the fact that it's Krstic calling, you know, is what I use to base my assessment that at this point in time that this conversation is occurring, Borovcanin is at the headquarters of the Bratunac Brigade and not at the civilian police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How do we know that the Bosnian Muslims are not intercepting radio or telephone communications from the police station?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, most of the police communications in that respect tended to go over already-established land lines of the PTT, which would make them more difficult for them to intercept. My knowledge of the intercept project and the various networks related to it reflect the fact that the PTT was a separate network from the military telecommunications network, and these intercepts that we're discussing at some juncture passed over the military network and thus made them liable for interception.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. We see this brief conversation. Krstic says: "How's it going?" Borovcanin says: "It's going well." Krstic says: "Don't tell me you have problems." Borovcanin says: "I don't, I don't." What is this, militarily, if anything, besides two friends chatting, or what do you make of this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I make of this General Krstic, who at this time has just become the commander of the Drina Corps, speaking with Borovcanin and getting a situation report from Borovcanin as to what has been occurring and whether or not his forces are having any issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where do you put the Kravica warehouse massacre, in terms of 2040 hours on this day?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding, again based on the investigation, is that the massacre began at 1700 hours and continued in spurts, or in pulses, so to speak, for an hour or two afterwards. This conversation occurs after most of the people in the Kravica warehouse are dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So do you incorporate that, if that's the case, would it be consistent, and if Borovcanin knew about that, since we know from the case that he was there with Petrovic, do you -- what do you make of him telling Krstic it's going well and that he doesn't have any problems, if anything?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, I mean, not only to infer these issues, you have to understand what Borovcanin was dealing with, you also have to note what General Krstic, himself, was personally aware of. And in that respect, I am aware that, you know, as part of the earlier investigation and as noted in testimony during the Krstic trial, that during the late afternoon hours, General Krstic, himself, did travel the road Bratunac-Konjevic Polje-Nova Kasaba-Milici in order to get to his headquarters at Vlasenica, first to begin the planning for the Zepa operation and, second, that's where he received his promotion to the commander of the Drina Corps. So General Krstic had a first-hand knowledge of the situation not only militarily along that road, but was aware by sight of the thousands of prisoners who were being taken. So in this context, and given that General Krstic is aware of that situation, that's how I read this particular intercept. He's aware that prisoners are being captured, that there is a plan to kill those prisoners, and he's discussing this issue with Borovcanin, both the military aspects of the security of the road as well as the killing of the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, we don't see any discussion about any killing going on here, so how do you -- how do you make that statement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With very few exceptions, you don't see references to the killing in documents or intercepts. It, again, goes back to the context of General Krstic being aware of General Mladic's order related to the fate of the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go on to the next document, which is an area that is a subject of the indictment which we have referred to, in the Prosecution, as the Milici patients and their situation. Have you reviewed documents and materials associated with the Milici -- what we call the Milici patients?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you give us a very brief outline of what you've learned from the documents and other materials about the -- tell us -- what I mean -- what am I referring to when I say Milici patients?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think are you referring to P1542A.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, A. That's correct. I haven't gotten to that yet, but that's what we're getting to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If Mr. Butler could give us the broader picture of what he's learned from the documents, the intercepts, and then we'll go through some of them.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. From my review of the documents, and, again, while I was part of the investigation team, there was evidence collected that reflected that on the evening of the 12th and through the 13th of July 1995, a number of Bosnian Muslim soldiers or military-aged men, who were captured by the VRS and the affiliated police forces, were wounded and in need of medical attention. A number of these individuals - I believe the number is approximately 13 or 14 - were sent to the medical facility in Milici, where they were treated by the doctors at that facility. Those patients, because very rapidly it taxed out the ability of the medical facility to care for them, were ultimately -- or were first transferred from the Medical Centre in Milici to the Medical Centre in Zvornik. They were subsequently transferred from the Medical Centre in Zvornik to the Zvornik Infantry Brigade, where they were then kept in that particular brigade's infirmary. At some point after they were transferred to the Zvornik Brigade Command and kept in the infirmary there, they disappeared and are currently missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let me first go to 65 ter 1316 and come back to the intercept we were looking at. But 1316, that's under tab 123.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this is a document that we see dated 24 July, and the Republika Srpska War Hospital Milici, to the Drina Corps Command, to General Krstic personally, entitled "Medical Support for Operation Srebrenica 95," and it's from the War Hospital director, Dr. Radomir Davidovic, neurosurgeon. Is this a document you've had a chance to review?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could just go to page 2 of the English, and it's probably the page 2 of the B/C/S as well. It's right near the bottom of the page, where the signature name is. In fact, it may be the next page in the B/C/S. Yes, I think -- well, I think we have to go one more page. Yeah, I think that's where this would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I just want to note -- I mean, we see, generally, as we look through this, it talks about medical support, and then very near the end he says: "Eighteen wounded enemy have undergone surgery and have been transferred to the hospital in Zvornik on the orders of the Main Staff." What do you think that is a reference to, given your knowledge of the investigation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a reference to wounded prisoners who were being treated at the Milici facility and then were subsequently transferred to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I would offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 1316 shall be assigned Exhibit P2532. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm going back to P1542A, this very short intercept between X and Y at 1236 hours, and this is on 13 July, from our intercept records.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We see X saying --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is a confidential document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- "Don't send me any more Muslims to Milici because the hospital is overcrowded. Send them to Zvornik." And it says: "All right. Professor Davidovic is down there, and he's been sending them." This other document we just saw was in the name of Dr. Radomir Davidovic, neurosurgeon. Can you connect this intercept and that other document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I believe the Professor Davidovic that they are talking about is, in fact, Dr. Davidovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And just one line I forgot to ask you about. When Dr. Davidovic says that 18 soldiers have been transferred to Zvornik, he says "on orders of the Main Staff," what do you make of that? How is it that the Main Staff is involved in 18 wounded Muslim soldiers?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the context of military operations, the Main Staff monitors all aspects of what's going on. As noted in Dr. Davidovic's reports, you know, there are a number of wounded soldiers coming in -- a fairly good number of wounded soldiers during the period coming in, and it's not -- not only is it not unreasonable; it would be a duty of at least medical members of the Main Staff and other organisation to be monitoring what is happening at the military medical facilities and ensuring that those facilities continue to have the capability to treat wounded and injured soldiers. At some point, Milici becomes overcrowded, and a decision is made by somebody at the Main Staff that in order to alleviate that overcrowding, the wounded prisoners will be sent from Milici to Zvornik, where, presumably, they had ample space at that time to deal with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, these 18 people -- wounded people that come to the Milici Hospital, are they coming from the same or a different area of captured prisoners than those over 1.000 prisoners that are mentioned in the Savcic memo, where, according to that memo, Savcic is saying that Tolimir is making proposals and talking about the over 1.000 prisoners located around Kasaba?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this juncture, I don't recall. I do know that the investigation has spoken with the doctor. It's been a number of years, so I don't recall what he said exactly as to where the prisoners came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What is the general area? Is the general area around Milici Hospital associated with the general area around Kasaba to Konjevic Polje, for example? Just help remind us of the geography.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, sir. I mean, from Milici, if you continue eastward along the highway, the next town of consequence is Nova Kasaba, and then beyond that is Konjevic Polje. So they are geographically linked by the highway.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go now to 65 ter 1318.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you recall, sir, whether the invest -- and not to be broadcast, please. Sir, were you aware from the investigation whether or not any of those Milici patients that we've been talking about were -- were there any records that those patients were -- provided to the investigation by the Milici Hospital?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I'm aware that at some juncture as part of the investigation, OTP investigators did go to the Milici Hospital and were able to obtain records which reflect the intake of the wounded Bosnian Muslims as well as medical records relating to the care that they received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And looking at this exhibit, are these, to your knowledge, records relating to those patients?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I would offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 1318 shall be assigned Exhibit P2533, admitted under seal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And staying with this same topic for a bit, can we go to 65 ter 326.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we'll see that this is an interim combat report from the Zvornik Brigade, dated 22 July, in the name of Vinko Pandurevic. To your knowledge, is Pandurevic back to the Zvornik Brigade now on the 22nd of July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Colonel Pandurevic arrives back in the brigade zone approximately noon on 15 July, and he remains there at least during this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I just want to ask you about this line in paragraph 3: "We request from the corps command that the Exchange Commission start work as soon as possible." And especially this line: "We also require instructions as to what to do with the prisoners, where to put them, and to whom we should hand them over." What do you make of this last line about asking for instructions, what to do with the prisoners, that we see that he's referring to some prisoners taken on the 22nd of July in this document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, as the investigation has borne out, the Zvornik Infantry Brigade has been taking prisoners daily as a result of its combat with the column. And with the exception of one prisoner, who happened to be a high-ranking communications official with the 28th Infantry Division, those prisoners are never accounted for and are presumed to have been killed shortly after capture at some juncture. Those types of prisoner accountings are not included in the daily combat reports of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade during the period. This combat report on the 22nd of July is the first written report from the Zvornik Brigade where they are talking about prisoners that they have killed -- or not prisoners that they have killed -- enemies that they have killed, i.e., liquidated, again using that phrase, as well as soldiers who are being captured, and only at this date, the 22nd of July, is the Zvornik Brigade requesting the Drina Corps Command provide guidance as to what to do with prisoners that they're capturing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So what? What's your point? Pardon the bluntness.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The point is: By the 22nd of July, the commander of the Zvornik Brigade understands that, We're not killing prisoners as we capture them anymore, and that, Since we're not doing that, I need instructions as to what I'm supposed to do with the prisoners that I am capturing. That is how I take this particular issue and the point behind it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. On a related point, since you've mentioned this, can you tell the Chamber -- and I believe this document's in evidence and they've seen it, but I don't need it up right now. Do you recall an 18 July report that Vinko Pandurevic sends to the Drina Corps, where he talks about Muslims coming to his area?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us your recollection of what he says and what you make of that, since I think it's relate to do what you've just said?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that particular report, that interim combat report of 18 July 1995, Colonel Pandurevic is sending to the Drina Corps a rather detailed discussion as to not only the issues related to combat that his unit has just undergone and the casualties that his unit has taken, not only in the Srebrenica battle, but in the previous months of combat, as well as raises the issue that, you know, in spite of everything else related to combat, his brigade had to deal with the -- I believe the number he uses is 2- or 3.000 prisoners that somebody made a decision to put in his brigade area. There's a rather complex back-story related to this interim combat report that I don't know that I need to go into, but these -- Colonel Pandurevic, again, his awareness of the prisoners, that they were brought into his zone, and what happened to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let me get back on point to the Milici patients, if we could. I'd offer that last document, 65 ter 326, into evidence. It refers to the question about what to do with prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to put one question to the witness in relation to this document. I see Pandurevic, in his report, mentions 23 Muslim soldiers captured, and then, in addition to that, the unit from Osmaci captured 17 Muslims along its own line. You were discussing the capturing of these prisoners, and you were referring to these altogether 40 captured Muslim soldiers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir. I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If you -- I would like to refer you to the second paragraph under item 1 of this document. I see there 10 enemy soldiers were liquidated, while 23 Muslim soldiers were captured. And then the next sentence, there's an indication that 17 Muslims were captured along its own line. All together, 40, I take it. And you were discussing this document, and you were especially referring to these 40 soldiers, captured soldiers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. This -- in this document, this is the first time that one sees, in a Zvornik Brigade combat report, a reference to Bosnian Muslims. These -- at this point, these are people who are now trapped behind the line and are being captured by -- the 23 by the Zvornik Brigade and, as you note, Tactical Group Osmaci, not technically part of the Zvornik Brigade, but an adjacent unit, and Colonel Pandurevic is aware of those as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This document will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 326 shall be assigned Exhibit P2534. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And one last question before the break, Mr. President, that Mr. Butler may or may not be able to help us with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, there's been evidence in this case that the first group of Srebrenica prisoners arrived at Batkovic from the Bratunac area on 18 July. You may remember that. Do you recall, aside from that 18 from Bratunac, what date we first see other Srebrenica prisoners start arriving at Batkovic, but if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recall from both documents and the conduct of the investigation, I believe those prisoners don't start arriving in Batkovic until the 24th or 25th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, we've got those records and we'll double-check them. And I think it's time for the break, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed. We will have our second break and resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could go to P850B, still on the topic of the -- no broadcast - of prisoners and Milici patients.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This should be an a intercept of 23 July, where Pandurevic, Vinko, is mentioned as a participant, and a question mark is for the person that he is talking to. And I just want to ask you, Mr. Butler, I know you've had a chance to review this, but what was see the first question: "How are you?" And Vinko Pandurevic says: "I'm all right, not too bad." Then someone says: "What's new with you?" Pandurevic says: "We are catching Turks still. I have prisoners ..." Now, this is -- as we see, it's a 23 July intercept at 0800 hours. Do you relate this comment by Pandurevic of "I have prisoners" with the -- it's the 22 interim combat report that we just went over, where he required instructions on what to do with prisoners?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He also says: "I have the wounded, so I don't know what to do with them, where to send them." Do you believe in this he's referring to wounded Serbs, or wounded Muslims, or can you tell ?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this context, it's my opinion he's referring to the wounded Muslims. I don't believe he would have any questions or doubts as to what he should be doing if they were his own soldiers who were wounded. There's well-established practices for how those people will be treated and where they will be evacuated to in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And from the investigation, are you aware of what wounded Muslims he would have -- had been referring to on this date, 23 July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. These would be the wounded Bosnian Muslims who had started in Milici, who were transferred to the Zvornik Medical Centre, and then were subsequently transferred to the Zvornik Brigade Infirmary at the Standard Garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And if we could go to what is marked as P85A, a conversation that happens at -- five minutes later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is it possible that it is P851?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I meant to say, Mr. President, 851A. We see the same conversation on this English translation, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's also confidential. It should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. So if we could go to P851A.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Five minutes after this conversation where Pandurevic asks about what to do with the wounded, it says: "The participant '?' in the previous conversation called and asked for Vinko again ..." So who would Vinko be in this conversation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be Vinko Pandurevic, the commander of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this participant noted as "?," that's the same way the previous person in the conversation was noted as, as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So we see: "The participant '?' in the previous conversation called and asked for Vinko again, but Ljubo answered, and '?' told Ljubo to pass on to Vinko." Now, "Ljubo," any idea who Ljubo is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who do you think Ljubo is? And I think we all understand at this point that Ljubo is a relatively common Serb name.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that he's referring to a staff officer on the Zvornik Brigade. If I recall correctly, his name is Ljubo Bojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And why do you -- why do you think this is Ljubo Bojanovic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He -- his name appears in other aspects of the investigation as the officer who was sent out from the Zvornik Brigade to relieve Drago Nikolic, who was performing functions as the duty officer of the Zvornik Brigade IKM, or forward command post, on the evening of 13 July 1995. And in that context, I'm familiar with his name as being a staff officer in the brigade, so he is the only one I'm aware of with the first name of Ljubo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you be mixing that up with Mihajlo Galic, on the 13th of July, from the IKM?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe so. It's been a while since I've looked at the IKM documents. I know he's not there on the 13th, I know he's there on subsequent days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's continue on in the intercept. It says -- what "?" says: "What Vinko and I were just talking about, will arrive at your place by 1700 hours. The boss, Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic, will arrive and say what needs to be done regarding the work we talked about." What do you make of that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Coupling this with the previous intercept and the role of Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic, I take it that Popovic will be coming up and will have some dealings with the prisoners that are being taken by the Zvornik Brigade, inclusive of the wounded prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now let's go to it should be P1459, and I have page 143.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is an entry from the Zvornik Brigade duty officer note-book for the period 23 July. Had you reviewed the duty officer note-book as part of your analysis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. With respect to my past testimonies, that particular document did not come into the possession of the OTP until after the publication of the revised narrative. But I have seen it since then, and I have read it, of course, and testified related to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I hope I've got the right numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you remind us who normally wrote many of the entries in the duty officer note-book?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Customarily, it was either the duty operations officer or one of his assistants. They were on duty -- they were, essentially, the 24-hour duty operations officers, and they would, and they would note information in the note-book that was important, relevant, passing of messages, things of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in looking at that short intercept that we just talked about that mentioned Ljubo, that "Ljubo answered," have you seen it where the duty officer on duty at the command answers the telephone, that is noted down by the intercept operators?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this should be page 142 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the English document we are looking at now is the version we call the teacher's edition, and it's the position of the Prosecution that the duty officer that day on the 23rd was Ljubo Bojanovic. Would that be consistent with your analysis that the previous intercept, P851A, the Ljubo mentioned would have been Ljubo Bojanovic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And that conversation, as we note, is noted at 0805 hours. And now, in the duty officer note-book, we see it as: "0830 hours. Lieutenant-Colonel Cerovic relayed a message for commander that Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic will arrive by 1500 [sic] hours."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think you misspoke. In the English translation, it says "1700 hours."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You're absolutely correct, Your Honour. I know it's 5.00, and I put a "5" in there. I apologise about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: 1700 hours, which, of course, is what we saw from the previous intercept. Do you relate this notation at all with the previous two intercepts?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. This is the duty officer's notation of the accounting of the previous two phone conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us who Lieutenant-Colonel Cerovic is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. He is the assistant commander of Morale, Religious and Legal Affairs for the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in your view, would he be any of the people or -- persons from the previous intercept, if you connect these two, like you say, who, if anyone, would he be?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you were able to connect all three, he would be the correspondent identified by the question mark.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And it says "relayed a message for commander." If Ljubo Bojanovic is a staff officer receiving this at the Zvornik Brigade, who would the reference to "commander" be, in your view?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be his commander, Lieutenant Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Lieutenant Colonel Popovic, in the context of this conversation with Cerovic passing on this message, who would Lieutenant-Colonel or "LTC" Popovic be?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is the chief of security for the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And let's go now to 65 ter 190.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this is a vehicle log for a Golf from Vlasenica. That's for July 1st through 31st July 1995. And under the box that says "Rank," and "Full name of driver/user," we first see "Dusan Vucic" [sic] and "Lieutenant-Colonel Vujadin Popovic." So can you tell from this front page who whose vehicle this should be on this day and this month?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looking at the context of the document, this monthly accounting sheet reflects that this vehicle operates under the direction of the security organ of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, perhaps you misspoke again. I see a different name of the driver, "Dusan Vucetic," and not "Vucic."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, you're absolutely correct. My Serbian lost a syllable there, and it is much easier than I made it sound. So you're correct, "Vucetic." And after 15 years, I have no excuse. I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But, Mr. Butler, can we go to the section in this document that is -- covers the use of the vehicle for 23 July, this date that we have been talking about related -- in the last few exhibits. I believe it's the fourth page in the English and the same in the B/C/S. And if we blow that up a little bit. I think we should be fine with the B/C/S because it's in Latin. We note that if we go to the 23rd, we see "Time used from," and it starts out at "0900 hours," that's all it says there, and then "7111," and then it describes the route "Vlasenica-Zvornik-Vlasenica." Is that consistent with the -- your analysis with regard to Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic going to the Zvornik Brigade to deal with prisoners and wounded?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It's evidence that he, in fact, did so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you remind us where the headquarters of the Drina Corps is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vlasenica, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I would offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 190 shall be assigned Exhibit P2535. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now we are getting back to our chronology, because the Milici patients took us a bit out of that chronology, but let's go back to P2143 -- or on to P2143, back to 13 July 1995, a Main Staff report to the president. And if we could go to page 3 in the English, page 3 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Under the section that says "The Enemy," looking at the part that talks about Srebrenica, it says: "The enemy from the former enclave of Srebrenica is in a state of total disarray, and the troops are surrendering in large numbers to the VRS. A 200- to 300-strong group of soldiers managed to break through the general sector of Mount Udrc, from where they are trying to break through to the territory under Muslim control." So the first part about this, that the enemy in Srebrenica -- the enemy from the former enclave is in total disarray and are surrendering in large numbers to the VRS; is that correct? Anything to add to that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. That's accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you've said who was in control of the area from Nova Kasaba to Konjevic Polje, and you've also said from Konjevic Polje to Kravica was MUP forces, so how would you explain that in this document, that those prisoners surrendering along the Konjevic Polje to the Kravica road? Were there VRS involved in those surrenders as well, do you know?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, the troops at Nova Kasaba and Konjevic Polje were members of the VRS. In this context, while technically they are surrendering to Special Police and not army soldiers, this is, again, a reflection that all of the combat forces there, to include the police forces, are operating under military control.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And going down to the situation in the corps, there's a mention of combat groups from other corps units are in the final stages of the preparation aimed at settling the issue of the Zepa enclave. Do you -- is that a correct statement in this report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. As the documents and other information sets out at the time, as this is occurring on the 13th, elements of the Zvornik Brigade, the Birac Brigade, and other associated army units are moving from the Srebrenica battle-front area to the Zepa area, where they are going to begin to undertake combat operations there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I note I forgot to ask you about this line in paragraph A, the part that I'd mentioned: "... a 200- to 300-strong group of soldiers managed to break through to the general sector of Mount Udrc." Now, you have just spoken at length, I believe, about the Muslims that broke through, and from the documents from the MUP. Does this 2- to 300 group, is that a different group? Is it the same group? Is this correct? What do you make of this reference that's going to the president?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe this is a manifestation of the situation that I talked about previously, where Major Obrenovic and other lower-level commanders of military and police units view these numbers as far higher, yet senior commanders at the Drina Corps and at the Main Staff are seeing a situation differently and have the numbers listed a lot lower. Just as I talk about in some cases commanders having a common view of the battle-field, this is an example where, you know, they don't have a common view of the battle-field. As it turns out, the Drina Corps and the Main Staff significantly underestimated the number of armed Muslim fighters in the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go now to P626.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this should take us back -- as I recall, Judge Nyambe asked you a question related to your knowledge about the whereabouts of Colonel Jankovic back in -- when you were talking about the 17th/18th of July documents and the MSF workers, it's my recollection, and you made a reference to something in your response to Her Honour. This particular document, what is it, and was that, in your recollection, related to anything that you gave to the Judge in answering her question, or am I mistaken on that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, this particular document is authored by Colonel Radoslav Jankovic from the Drina Corps forward command post in Bratunac. On the 13th of July, it lays out his knowledge and report back to the Main Staff of the situation regarding the evacuation of the entire Muslim population, the status of wounded prisoners, and lays out what he anticipates will be occurring in the upcoming days, or at least in this case the 14th, and proposals that he has made. He -- from the videotape evidence related to the meetings, he is in Bratunac as early as 13 July -- I'm sorry, as early as 11 July 1995. And to my knowledge, again based on documents and investigation, he remains in Bratunac during this entire period, dealing with these respective types of issues. I don't remember the exact details of Her Honour's questions, so I am not sure whether I responded to it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Does this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: It's not a question. It's just to retrace my own recollection of what was talked about at that point. I think your reference, as I understood it, was a reference to the Secretary-General's report on the fall of Srebrenica, I thought, but ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think in that context, we were talking about air power and things of that nature, so, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: My memory is -- we'll check the record and make sure we get that straight, Your Honour, and make that -- maybe Mr. Gajic's memory is better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: He's a young man. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I'm not mistaken, and I believe I do recall this well, this was to do with a document which bore the initials of Mr. Jankovic. It was a handwritten document. And there was another identical document that had a typewritten "Momir Nikolic" signature, and I believe that this is document led to the discussion that we are now trying to recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for this assistance. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. And in that discussion, I recall Mr. Butler saying something along the lines of, Yes, you will -- we will have seen documents from previous days from Colonel Jankovic. So thank you. I think it will be made clear. Thank you very much, Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Just one -- one question about this. We see that he is talking about, in the middle of paragraph 1, that there are 54 wounded at the UNPROFOR base, a list of names has been taken from the UNPROFOR, a doctor from the UNPROFOR has stayed in the hospital in Bratunac, at the request of the hospital staff, to make sure that the patients are properly treated. It says: "I intend to send him away tomorrow, under the pretext that his help is not necessary." Do you have any information or any knowledge of what he's talking about here, why he would need a pretext or why he has a pretext to send away a doctor that's looking after patients?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would need to invent a pretext to send the doctor away, claiming his help was not necessary, if it is his intention that he does not want Dutch or other international observers to be in a position to see and monitor what is happening with those particular group of wounded prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As far as you can recall from the investigation, were the -- this group of prisoners eventually transported to Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. With the exception of one of the wounded prisoners who was identified as a suspect in crimes against Serbs and placed in police custody, the remaining prisoners were transported to Batkovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you remember if that one person you talked about survived?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, he -- in fact, because he was in police custody, he did survive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember his name?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's been some time since I've seen that particular document. No, sir, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And on that same topic, when we were talking about the local staff for MSF and the UNMO staff - that was the discussion of the -- both in the documents and the intercepts - and they were listed in the intercept, and finally we saw the document that listed their names from the MSF, I failed to ask you: Did the investigation reveal whether those men and some women survived?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. If I recall correctly, all those individuals were ultimately allowed to depart from the former enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. All right. Could we go to P1225.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see a document here from the Drina Corps Command at the now forward command post called Krivace, dated 13 July, speaking of some Srebrenica events. And on that first English page and the B/C/S, we see: "Combat readiness at 8.00 a.m." or "800 hours on 14 July." We see the Krivace Command Post and some things, and on the next page in the English, the command post in the village of Podzeplje, and various other tasks and things. What is this? And it's in the name of, excuse me, Major-General Radislav Krstic.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just as Krivaja-95 was the name of the detailed operations plan related to Srebrenica, this document is the detailed operations plan relating to what would be VRS military operations against the Zepa enclave. In a near-identical manner to how the army laid out all of its objectives and tasks for individual units for Srebrenica, it does the same thing for Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see, on the first page, it appears to be handwritten "Military Secret, Stupcanica-95." What's that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the designated code-name for the Zepa operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Does this have anything to do with the order from General Mladic that you will recall us seeing - I believe it was dated 10 July - about getting ready for Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. To -- to some degree it is, because it details tasks for some of those units that he had previously given orders to on 10 July in order to prepare or create the circumstances to begin these operations. So in the military planning process, you have General Mladic already thinking about the next objective even before the first objective has been taken. And as the situation dealing with the first objective, Srebrenica, comes to pass, he is already rapidly transitioning the military forces, through his order and through that planning process that's being undertaken at the Main Staff in the Drina Corps, to move on to the next objective in an extremely rapid manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go on to the next document. It's 65 ter 109.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this is, we can see, an order from the Drina Corps, dated 13 July, entitled "Search of the Terrain," to various brigades. I won't read it. We see that it's in the name of -- and it says "Commander Major-General Radislav Krstic," and we see a stamp at 13 July, 20 [sic] hours, and then below that, "13 July, 2030 hours." At the time of the execution of this document or when it was made, in your view, was General Krstic the chief of staff of the Drina Corps or was he the commander of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time this document was created and signed, General Krstic had just been appointed the commander of the Drina Corps, replacing General Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you, as part of the investigation, learn from any witness or witnesses, or documents, the circumstances or the place upon which General Krstic was made commander of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did. As a component of the investigation and trial of General Krstic, one of his primary defences was that he was not the corps commander, so there was a significant priority placed on gathering evidence related to when, where, and how he assumed command. As a result of the evidence obtained, it reflects that General Mladic appointed General Krstic as the commander of the Drina Corps at approximately 2000 hours on 13 July 1995 at the corps headquarters in Vlasenica, and, in fact, did so on the signed orders of President Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I see that we've reached the end of the day, and there is a trial after ours, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you, at this point in time, tendering this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I should. I still have a question on this topic, but, no, I actually -- yes, I would tender this, please. Thank you for reminding me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 109 shall be assigned Exhibit P2536. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We have to adjourn for the week, and we will resume on Monday, 2.15 in the afternoon, in this courtroom. And, again, Mr. Butler, no contact with either party about the content of your testimony during this break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 18th day of July, 2011, at 2.15 p.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.46 p.m.,
